It is powered by Euro-Office, a European-led fork of the ONLYOFFICE codebase. Users can create, open and edit files locally without running a server or connecting to the internet, or connect to Nextcloud Hub to access cloud files and collaborate in real time. The suite includes word-processing, spreadsheet, presentation and PDF tools, with support for Microsoft Office formats DOCX, XLSX and PPTX as well as OpenDocument formats. items.title: [daverupert.com] Conventional Commit rules everything around me
items.content_html:
There’s a community standard out there called Conventional Commit for structured git-commit messages. If you don’t know about it already, it recommends a strict type(scope?): description format for describing a code change in a repo.

A normal git commit history might look like this:

> git log --oneline

9d30ff6 fix typo
3062496 oops
d0b38ad shit
b5f8df7 redesign site

That’s all well and good, but lacks a bit of structure and detail for a big project with lots of contributors. That’s where Conventional Commit comes in. Instead of a git-commit message like add login page, it might look like this:

feat: add user login endpoint

Or you can “scope” it to a particular section of your application:

feat(auth): add user login endpoint

There’s even a ! flag to signal a breaking change to your coworkers:

feat!: remove all authentication API endpoints

The predefined conventional commit types cover most types of changes: fix:, feat:, chore:, docs:, style:, refactor:, perf:, test:, build:, and ci:. I find these cover most situations but I’m also a bad boy and like to break rules, so I’ll throw in custom types like wip:, a11y:, hotfix:, or an rm: (as a treat) when I feel it adds clarity to the work.

But why would anyone voluntarily conform to a standard like this? My answer is… a feeling. Look at our git-log history now:

> git log --oneline

9d30ff6 fix(input): restore focus state on input
3062496 style(checkbox): update tokens to tokens v2
d0b38ad chore: update dependencies via dependabot
b5f8df7 feat(auth): add user login endpoint
...

In a noisy repo that’s increasingly getting noisier (thanks, robots) anywhere you can add predictability is a net-positive. The cumulative effect over time is that you have a highly-scannable, uniform history of what’s happening in your project.

Conventional Commit can even help with code review. A style: fix that adds dozens of npm packages should be a signal that you need to break up the work. Types might also inform if you route all a11y: commits to the local expert for code review. And a refactor! breaking change should signal coworkers to be extra-cautious in review and may trigger other process-oriented workflows like broadcasting the upcoming breaking change to anyone in the blast radius.

And because it’s a community standard, like the Custom Element Manifest, you can build tooling around it like commitlint. As its name implies, commitlint is a linter that gates all commit messages from your entire team to ensure they abide in the type(scope): description format. I personally tend to avoid adding extra tooling to enforce simple conventions, but I might change my mind on this because the benefits start compounding.

If my commits were all similarly formatted, I could also automate our entire changelog and semantic versioning bumps for releases.

  • fix: = PATCH
  • feat: = MINOR
  • any!: = MAJOR

Of course, Conventional Commit and Semver itself aren’t perfect but it adds a degree of predictability about the impact of a change from the description alone. Abiding in the Conventional Commit format is a small micro-adjustment to my process, but it has potential to positively impact the entire project and I like those sorts of zero-dollar improvements.

Extending Conventional Commit beyond commits

One place you’ll also want to extend conventional commit to is pull request titles. Not technically a git-commit message, but if you squash and merge commits the PR title tends to become the commit message by default. Preferring or enforcing conventional commit in pull request titles helps preserve our pristine commit history.

If you’re doing pull request titles, why not use them for issue titles too:

#123 > bug(input): required focus indcator missing
#122 > feat(checkbox): update tokens to v2
#112 > chore: update dependencies from depdendabot
#106 > feat(input): make input more engaging

There’s harmony when the issue and the solution are matching. Having the type in the issue title sets a clear deliverable; a bug: needs a fix: to resolve it. Consider these duplicate issues for the same bug:

#189 > 4.2.7 Focus Visible [bug] [components] [severity:HIGH]
#210 > bug(input): focus indicator is missing

Which one would get picked up first? I’d argue that even with labels like [bug] and [severity:HIGH] that the second one would be easier to fix because it gives the developer almost all the information they need to fix the issue.

It makes the issue a little more actionable and that’s what you want. If every issue is an investigation, nothing gets done. Triaging issues takes cognitive bandwidth. Labels are great at grouping and providing queryable views, but when scanning a list of issues pairing both the tag and the title to determine the ask adds an extra cognitive tax.

I’m projecting here, but uniform data in your PRs and issue queues could also allow you to collect stats on which components or areas of your application are the most buggy and expensive to maintain. It can tell you who’s getting saddled with all the bugs or which issue filer is adding too much feature debt. And it can help your team quantify your recurring maintenance tasks that might be hiding because it gets rolled into other work. That might be valuable to an organization.

Unconventional usage of Conventional Commit

Now let’s extend beyond the practical. I’m finding the Conventional Commit format to be so useful, I’ve started rolling them out to a lot of different places (surprise, coworkers!).

One example is our folder full of random scripts/ in the monorepo. What was a randomized list of dozens of scripts and tests…

scripts/
├── docs-tokens.mjs
├── playwright-cli.mjs
├── storybook-compat-table.mjs
├── style-dictionary.mjs
├── sync-fluent-fluent-custom-elements-manifest.mjs
├── validate-themes.mjs
└── visual-review-harness.mjs

Can become an organized paradise of co-located responsibility:

scripts/
├── build/
│   └── themes-style-dictionary.mjs
├── docs/
│   ├── storybook-generate-compat-table.mjs
│   ├── tokens-generate-table.mjs
│   └── sync-fluent-custom-elements-manifest.mjs
└── test/
    ├── playwright-cli.mjs
    └── playwright-visual-review-harness.mjs
    └── themes-validator.mjs

I’ve found those Conventional Commit types tend to map well to areas of responsibility for repo-level scripts. Manage docs, tests, build tasks, and so on all fit under the Conventional Commit umbrella and it adds some much needed organization to the junk drawer of copy-pasta and generated helper scripts.

And if your scripts/ folder is following the Conventional Commit format… why not roll that out to your scripts in package.json:

{ 
  "scripts": {
	  "docs:generate": "node ./scripts/docs/generate-storybook-compat-table.mjs && node ./scripts/docs/generate-storybook-tokens-table.mjs",
	  "build:themes": "node ./scripts/build/themes-style-dictionary.mjs",
	  "test:themes": "node  ./scripts/test/themes-validator.mjs"
  }
}

Built-in npm features like pre* and post* hooks mess up our perfect naming system a bit. A prebuild:themes task reads fine but predocs:generate is a bit marble-mouthy. But that’s an eye-twitching discrepancy I’m willing to accept to abide in what npm gives me for free.

Then… if you’ve added Conventional Commit to your scripts/ and your "scripts" and are living that agentic coding life, why not apply the same organization principle to your skills/ folder?

skills/
├── build/
│   ├── themes/SKILL.md
├── docs/
│   ├── component-jsdoc/SKILL.md
│   ├── storybook/SKILL.md
│   └── technical-writing/SKILL.md
└── test/
    ├── playwright-tests/SKILL.md
    ├── visual-tests/SKILL.md
    └── writing-tests/SKILL.md

This looks great… it falls apart in the real world. Skills installed from the internet don’t abide in this format. Having some skills nested and others not creates a feeling of unease, so a flatter folder structure for skills is probably better. That said, it’s not uncommon to need a skill to inform your model about your repo-level scripts and those are places you can still maintain parity.

skills/
├── build-themes/SKILL.md
├── docs-storybook/SKILL.md
├── docs-components/SKILL.md
├── docs-technical-writing/SKILL.md
├── grill-me/SKILL.md
├── i-have-adhd/SKILL.md
├── test-playwright/SKILL.md
├── test-visual-review/SKILL.md
└── test-writing/SKILL.md

While applying Conventional Commit to your skills/ folder is a bit impractical, one area I can confirm it does help is organizing your agent chats. Fire off a handful of agents and it can get confusing about which one is doing what task, even with their autogenerated chat label. I’ve found it super helpful to ask your bot to rename its chat using the Conventional Commit format.

Try it out and bask in the uniform list of tasks. To get this to work consistently in the GitHub Copilot app, I had to modify my session prompt in Sessions > App instructions:

At the start of every new chat, before answering my first request, 
call `rename_session` using `type(scope): description`. Do this even 
for non-coding chats. Rename only once unless I ask otherwise.

I’m not sure how it works in your preferred agent manager, but I assume you could write a skill or put it in your AGENTS.md, but I’d have a conversation with your coworkers first before codifying your obsessive-compulsions in the project repo.

Join me in my obsession

You might have read all this and said, “This is a man who –in a world of chaos– is looking to over-manage a small thing like title text so that he can feel in control of his own life!” and to that I’d say…

Probably.

I like to think I’ve just hit the point in my life where I don’t want to spend an single brain cell thinking about how I should format title text or name a file. I wasn’t this passionate about Conventional Commit a year ago, I think I got radicalized. Generative AI almost certainly plays a big part where every robot names files and fixes different every time. That’s built-in to its dice-roll mechanic. Knowing there’s a chaos agent in the mix, I feel a need to find low-hanging fruit for consistency and (for right now) this feels pretty good to me.

items.title: [MacRumors] Apple Shares HomeView 27.2 Release Notes With List of Features
items.content_html:
Apple's new HomeView smart home display launched today and the release notes for HomeView software version 27.2 are now available in a support document.


Since these are the first HomeView release notes that Apple has publicly shared, they go over a lot of the device's basic features and functionality:
HomeView software delivers powerful, personalized experiences to enjoy entertainment, stay connected, and manage your smart home. It features a conversational Siri AI that helps you find what you need and get things done. And with multiuser recognition, customizable faces, and deep Apple ecosystem integration, up to six members of your household get content and controls tailored just for them.

Siri AI

  • A more capable and conversational version of Siri that helps you find what you need and get more done

  • Personal context understanding draws on your Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone to help you find what you're looking for, like that recipe your mother emailed you

  • Broad world knowledge lets you ask questions about virtually any topic and get a detailed answer

  • Rich content discovery makes it easy to find new music and podcasts using natural language

  • HomeView and Siri AI on HomeView are available in English, and require your paired iPhone or iPad to be set to the same English variant¹,²



Entertainment

  • Apple Music lets you enjoy your favorite songs with animated lyrics and Spatial Audio support, alongside easy search and browse capabilities

  • Podcasts lets you enjoy audio and video shows with transcripts and personalized recommendations

  • Apple TV, Apple News, and Audiobooks let you use your iPhone to enjoy your favorite shows, catch up on daily audio stories, or get lost in a good book

  • Supported third-party audio and video apps installed on your iPhone automatically appear on HomeView

  • Multiroom audio allows you to play and control music in sync across multiple HomeView, HomePod, and AirPlay speakers



Connection

  • FaceTime makes it easy to connect with loved ones hands-free, using Center Stage to keep you perfectly framed even as you move around the room

  • Messages lets you easily read and reply to texts using Siri, the onscreen keyboard, or Tapback

  • Intercom allows you to broadcast messages across your home, to specific rooms, or to personal Apple devices

  • Safari lets you browse the web and includes a new Cooking experience that auto-detects supported recipes, reformatting them with step-by-step instructions and inline timers

  • Find My lets you view the location of friends and family, or locate misplaced Apple devices and AirTags

  • Handoff makes it easy to seamlessly move audio, video, websites, or calls directly from your iPhone to HomeView



Home Control

  • Home Modular face offers a concise, glanceable look at your home accessories

  • Home Camera face allows you to livestream up to nine simultaneous camera feeds

  • Home app gives you a dedicated dashboard to control accessories and activate scenes across your entire house

  • Home hub capabilities keep you connected to your HomeKit and Matter accessories, allow you to control your home while away, and enable automations

  • Sound Recognition detects the sounds of smoke and carbon monoxide alarms and alerts you on personal devices like your iPhone, iPad, or Apple Watch



Personalized Experiences

  • Customizable faces let you personalize your space with curated photos, modular home controls, and playful animations like Snoopy

  • Seamless recognition identifies up to six different users by face and voice, instantly displaying their specific Home Screen layout, widgets, and personal content

  • Personal content³ like Messages and Calendar is designed to stay private and be displayed when an enrolled user is recognized, and their recently unlocked iPhone or iPad is present and on the same network

  • Guest experience lets unrecognized people play media and control smart home accessories without accessing a user's personal content


1. Available in English. Spanish language support to come.
2. Some features may not be available in all regions or languages. Some devices may not be available in all regions. Siri AI is available in beta in HomeView software version 27.2. Personal context requests require a paired Apple Intelligence–enabled iPhone or iPad running the latest software version with Siri AI turned on and set to a supported language. Certain Apple Intelligence features that rely on server-side models are subject to daily usage limits. Expanded access to such features will be available for a fee in the future. Use of these features is subject to the Apple Intelligence Terms and Conditions. Learn more.
3. Requires the user to be recognized by their face, and the paired iPhone or iPad must be recently unlocked and connected to the same Wi-Fi network. If disconnected from Wi-Fi, the device must have an active cellular connection in the same location and have recently connected to the same network.

items.title: [phoronix.com] Linux developer releases XRAID parity RAID integrated with XFS
items.content_html: Linux developer Christoph Hellwig has released XRAID, a declustered parity RAID implementation integrated with the XFS file system and designed especially for zoned storage devices such as shingled magnetic recording drives. XRAID also works with conventional hard drives and SSDs. Early figures cited by Hellwig indicate writes can be up to 20 times faster than Linux’s mdraid, though SSD performance was not a focus. The code has been in development for 18 months and is available for wider testing, but Hellwig said it is not ready for submission to the Linux kernel. Its kernel patches are under review on the mailing list, while an xfsprogs branch supports file-system creation and provides a new management utility.

items.title: [phoronix.com] Linux 7.5 adds driver for FPGA-based Glanda GPU design
items.content_html: Linux kernel graphics developers have queued a driver for GlandaGPU, an open-source graphics processor design for field-programmable gate array (FPGA) hardware, for Linux 7.5. The driver is included in a DRM-Misc-Next pull request sent Nov. 13, ahead of the kernel’s merge window, which is expected to begin in late December. GlandaGPU is designed for learning and open-source demonstrations rather than demanding graphics work: it provides 640-by-480 VGA output and 2D acceleration. The pull request also includes support for an Allwinner processor’s VIP9000 graphics core and cursor-plane support for Hyper-V.

items.title: [macrumors.com] Apple launches $299 HomeView smart display ahead of Siri fixes
items.content_html: Apple began selling HomeView, its first smart display, on Friday, Nov. 13, for $299 in eight countries, excluding the European Union because Siri AI is not available there. The 7-inch device combines smart-home controls, video calls, music and personalized information for up to six household members, but its personal features depend on a nearby iPhone or iPad. Reviews praised the aluminum design, screen and tabletop model’s sound, while criticizing the lack of an App Store, restricted third-party apps and uneven Siri performance. Some testers also found that personal messages could remain visible to other household members after a user walked away. Apple released HomeView Software 27.2 on Nov. 12 with security fixes for nine vulnerabilities and said a December update would let recognized users ask Siri to unlock compatible doors and garage doors. The planned update will also fix Siri’s incorrect claim that the device has no camera, Apple told technology journalist Joanna Stern.

The company said it will continue to support existing cameras, doorbells, and other products. How long software, cloud services, and security updates will remain available is unclear. Fox completed its $22 billion acquisition of the streaming company on November 6. Roku entered the smart home business in 2022 with cameras, lights, and plugs. In the third quarter of 2026, device revenue increased 33 percent year over year. At the same time, losses in the device business rose from $22.9 million to $48.6 million; Roku pointed mainly to higher memory costs. By then, only two smart home products were available in its online store.

items.title: [simon42.com] Hands-on test: Nabu Casa’s AUX-2 plays in sync with Sendspin, but responds with a delay
items.content_html: A hands-on test by 少数派 on November 12 showed that the Home Assistant Connect AUX-2 plays music reliably in sync, but responds with a delay when starting playback and switching tracks. Nabu Casa’s €59 adapter connects older audio devices to the smart home. In the test, several speakers remained synchronized for hours after playback started; when creating or dissolving a group, the system responded more slowly than Apple’s AirPlay. The review recommends a wired network connection: playing lossless FLAC files over Wi-Fi may cause dropouts on heavily congested 2.4 GHz networks. The author suggests the Opus codec as an alternative, since it requires less bandwidth. The AUX-2 connects conventional speakers via Music Assistant and the open Sendspin protocol; passive speakers still require an amplifier.

items.title: [Bambu Lab Community Forum - Latest posts] Should we embrace the layer lines instead of trying to hide them?
items.content_html:
DWdesigns:

It may take some time for the general public to embrace the layner lines as part of a maker-made vibe, but we creators can take them as what they are - a natural feature of the FDM printing.

I think we are comfortable at the point where makers can treat 3D printing as another tool in their arsenal rather than as a gimmick. We (well, many of you more than myself) know what our printers can excel at, and what the limitations still are. Prints that make the best use of the FDM method speak for themselves! So yes, I fully agree, a good print may have layer lines, but those lines are just a natural product of 3D printing, and not a flaw at all.

I can’t help but notice we are seeing more and more prints that have stopped trying to reproduce other building methods (injected, woodworking, sheet metal, whatever) and embrace the power and uniques that FDM provides. In doing so, the weaknesses of trying to use the printer as a hammer are going away. I really like how much people are putting artwork into the prints more now. I just saw @Josh-3D 's drum print. I can’t imagine who sees that in real life is going to decide that layer lines are detracting from how cool it is!

items.title: [community.home-assistant.io] Nabu Casa launches AUX-2 for €59 to connect smart-home devices
items.content_html: Nabu Casa has unveiled the Home Assistant Connect AUX-2. The €59 box connects older hi-fi systems and compatible TVs, inverters, or heating devices to a Home Assistant system. The device has been available worldwide since November 11 and offers two serial RS-232 ports, Bluetooth LE, an audio output, and USB-A. Power over Ethernet (PoE) or USB-C and Wi-Fi are available for power and network connectivity. Home Assistant can control supported devices locally through the serial ports. Music Assistant outputs music through existing amplifiers and is intended to synchronize playback with compatible speakers. A Bluetooth proxy can connect sensors; the USB port can be used to operate a Z-Wave adapter at a more suitable location on the network. The AUX-2 requires a running Home Assistant system and uses the open platform ESPHome. Nabu Casa provides the configuration on GitHub. The AUX-2 lets users continue using supported devices or control them without a manufacturer’s cloud service. However, the box does not replace arbitrary device integrations: serial control works only with supported devices, and Zigbee via the AUX-2 is still considered experimental. Nabu Casa lists a price of $69 or €59; independent reviews point to cheaper DIY or alternative solutions.

items.title: [9to5google.com] Google fixes Nest camera bug and expands Gemini controls
items.content_html: Since November 11, Google has been rolling out an update for the Google Home app that is intended to fix Live View outages on five older Nest camera models migrated to the app and improve smart home controls with Gemini. Affected models include the wired first-generation Nest Doorbell, first-generation Nest Cam Indoor and Outdoor, and both Nest Cam IQ models. The fix affects certain connections, including PPPoE, fiber, and mobile hotspots; event recordings continued during Live View outages. Gemini can ask follow-up questions about ambiguous device commands, manage timers faster, and display relevant images alongside answers on Nest Hub displays. The update also adds a shared energy-saving mode for multiple Nest thermostats and digital house keys in Google Wallet for compatible Aliro locks. Google is rolling out the update gradually; the keys are initially available in Public Preview, and several Gemini features are available only to Early Access users.

items.title: [3dprinting.com] SINTX completes 3D-printing facility, targets implant availability in 2027
items.content_html: SINTX Technologies has completed its 3D-printing facility and received medical-grade EXT-220 MED printers to develop patient-specific implants made from silicon nitride and PEEK, a polymer used in orthopedic devices. The Salt Lake City company says the platform is intended to combine PEEK’s structural and imaging properties with silicon nitride’s biological properties. SINTX expects to receive compounded filament from Evonik before the end of 2026 and is pursuing U.S. Food and Drug Administration clearance for a defined range of extremity implants. It is evaluating limited custom-device opportunities in the first quarter of 2027. Broader distribution will depend on regulatory clearances and manufacturing validation.

items.title: [simon42.com] AI tool HA-MCP arrives in the Home Assistant Marketplace and requires admin privileges
items.content_html:
🌲 🏔️ ✏️

The community project HA-MCP can be installed directly through the integrated Marketplace starting with Home Assistant 2026.11. It connects AI assistants such as Claude and ChatGPT to Home Assistant and enables not only device control but also the creation and modification of automations, scripts, and dashboards. Previously, installation required a separate HACS entry. With version 9.0.0 on October 28, the server was integrated into Home Assistant. HA-MCP requires administrator privileges; the developers recommend a separate account restricted to local access. Remote access and access from the home network are initially disabled. For Home Assistant 2026.8 through 2026.10, HACS remains the installation method.

items.title: [blog.damonkohler.com] Running D&D Out of an Obsidian Vault
items.content_html: <p>A whole campaign — its maps, its monsters, its months of session history — fits in a folder of plain Markdown files. No database, no proprietary format, no subscription. The vault is the single source of truth, and everything else is a render, an export, or a link out to a platform.</p> <p>That constraint is the whole trick. Because every note is just text, the campaign gets a wikilink graph, structured database views, and an AI rendering pipeline almost for free — and it outlasts whatever note-taking app is fashionable next year.</p> <h2 id="the-vault-is-the-only-source-of-truth">The vault is the only source of truth<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#the-vault-is-the-only-source-of-truth" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Everything lives in one Obsidian vault: campaign notes, NPC cards, monster stat blocks, loot, location descriptions, and a running session log. Every proper noun in the campaign is a wikilink — a bracketed reference that jumps straight to the note it names. Write “the party enters the mine” in a session log and it links to the location note, where the read-aloud text, the encounter, and the DM-only secrets are already waiting.</p> <p>That graph is the feature that pays off most at the table. A player asks about someone they met three sessions ago, you type the name, and the note is right there. No searching, no flipping through a notebook.</p> <h2 id="organized-by-place-not-by-date">Organized by place, not by date<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#organized-by-place-not-by-date" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The vault is organized spatially, not chronologically. Each campaign is a self-contained folder, and inside it the notes follow a taxonomy borrowed from RPG video games — you travel to a place, you track an objective, you play through a scripted beat:</p> <ul> <li><strong>The campaign file</strong> is the novel: the planned story, its acts, and the plot threads still in play. It says what <em>could</em> happen.</li> <li><strong>Location notes</strong> are the zones. Each one describes a persistent place — the geography, the exits, who is present, the map — plus an index of what happens there.</li> <li><strong>Quest notes</strong> are the quest log. Each is an objective with a giver, a checklist of stages, a completion condition, and a reward. Some are critical-path, some are optional.</li> <li><strong>Scene notes</strong> are the cutscenes: the granular run-script for one beat. A trigger, the read-aloud text, a couple of skill checks, the branches, the tactical map, and a checkbox for each beat as it plays out.</li> <li><strong>The DM log</strong> is a scratchpad — one line per session recording where things left off.</li> <li><strong>Reference cards</strong> hold the NPCs, monsters, and loot for quick lookup during play.</li> </ul> <p>The key move is that run-scripts do not live inside the location note. A location is the <em>place</em>; the beats that unfold in it are separate scenes. Pulling the scripts out keeps each note short enough to parse at a glance mid-session, when you have no time to scroll.</p> <p>Those note types are wired together through wikilinks and metadata back-links into a spine: a quest stage names the locations and scenes it touches, a scene names the location it happens in, and a location indexes the scenes and quests that reach it. Any note is discoverable from its neighbors, so nothing goes missing under pressure.</p> <h2 id="database-views-do-the-bookkeeping">Database views do the bookkeeping<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#database-views-do-the-bookkeeping" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Obsidian Bases turn note metadata into database views — tables and cards built by querying the frontmatter, the small block of key-value fields at the top of each note. A party base shows armor class, hit points, initiative, and passive perception in one glanceable table during combat. An XP tracker pulls from every character note and computes what each one needs for the next level. The numbers live in each character’s frontmatter; the base only queries and displays them, so there is nothing to keep in sync by hand.</p> <h2 id="the-art-is-ai-made-the-direction-is-yours">The art is AI-made; the direction is yours<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#the-art-is-ai-made-the-direction-is-yours" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The battlemaps, monster tokens, NPC portraits, and atmospheric scenes are AI-made; the creative direction stays yours. A few small Python scripts call Google’s Gemini API, and each render is driven by a prompt written as a Markdown file kept in the vault alongside the content it illustrates — the prompt is where the direction lives, versioned like everything else. What used to take hours per map now takes minutes, so far more of the campaign gets art at all.</p> <p>Maps get one extra trick. You describe the layout in Markdown and include a DOT graph — a plain-text description of a graph, where nodes are areas and edges are the connections between them, with edge styles marking a path as normal, significant, or hidden. The model renders the art from the description; a second pass strips out any text and labels; then a precise grid, a scale bar, and column labels are overlaid to produce two copies. A DM version carries area labels and encounter markers. A clean player version is built for fog-of-war — a single image the virtual tabletop can mask and reveal as the party explores.</p> <p>The graph is what makes it work. Without it, the model produces beautiful art with nonsensical spatial relationships: rooms that should connect do not, or corridors loop in ways that break the game. The graph pins down the topology and lets the model handle only the aesthetics.</p> <p>Tokens, portraits, and scenes run a simpler path. A shared style instruction keeps a consistent dark-fantasy look across the whole campaign — monsters as full illustrations plus small circular tokens for the tabletop, NPCs as waist-up portraits plus tokens, and mood images for locations that want atmosphere rather than a battle grid.</p> <p>The result is not hand-drawn quality. It is consistent across the entire campaign and good enough for play, which is the trade that matters.</p> <h2 id="dd-beyond-holds-the-mechanics">D&D Beyond holds the mechanics<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#dd-beyond-holds-the-mechanics" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>Obsidian handles the flavor, the tactics, and the DM notes; the mechanical stat blocks live in D&D Beyond. Each monster and loot note carries a D&D Beyond URL in its frontmatter, so you jump from the narrative description straight to the rollable stat block. A browser-automation tool pushes vault homebrew up to the platform, rollable dice tags included — so “2d6 fire damage” becomes clickable dice on the character sheet. No copy-pasting stat blocks between two systems that both want to be right.</p> <h2 id="a-prep-pass-start-to-finish">A prep pass, start to finish<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#a-prep-pass-start-to-finish" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>A prep pass follows the notes rather than fighting them:</p> <ol> <li>Read the campaign file for active threads and guess what the party does next.</li> <li>Open the location and scene notes in play; write or revise the read-aloud text, place encounters, and set skill-check DCs.</li> <li>Generate any new combat encounters, balanced to the current party.</li> <li>Render the maps, tokens, portraits, and scene art the new content needs.</li> <li>Create or update the monster and NPC cards, then push their homebrew to D&D Beyond.</li> <li>Run a link-and-structure audit to catch broken wikilinks and missing notes before they surface at the table.</li> <li>Skim the party base for the numbers you will want on hand during play.</li> </ol> <p>During the session, you keep the scene note open and work down it, ticking checkboxes as each beat is revealed. Afterward, you add one line to the DM log and fold any improvised content back into the canonical notes, so the vault stays true the next time the party comes through.</p> <h2 id="its-just-files">It’s just files<a role="anchor" aria-hidden tabindex="-1" data-no-popover href="#its-just-files" class="internal"><svg width="18" height="18" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"><path d="M10 13a5 5 0 0 0 7.54.54l3-3a5 5 0 0 0-7.07-7.07l-1.72 1.71"></path><path d="M14 11a5 5 0 0 0-7.54-.54l-3 3a5 5 0 0 0 7.07 7.07l1.71-1.71"></path></svg></a></h2> <p>The payoff is that none of it is locked up. Markdown, images, and a few scripts — it syncs across devices as ordinary files and it will outlast whatever note-taking app is trendy next year. The encounter generation, the homebrew publishing, and the vault cleanup are small AI-driven tools bolted onto that plain-text core, not the thing that holds it together.</p> <p>It’s files all the way down, and that is exactly why it works.</p>

items.title: [smarthomeassistent.de] Loxone closes critical restart vulnerability in Miniserver with update
items.content_html: On November 10, Loxone released software version 17.3.11.10 for its home automation control unit, the Miniserver. The critical security update closes a vulnerability that allowed the Miniserver to be repeatedly restarted over the network. During such a restart loop, it can control neither lighting nor heating nor shading. The manufacturer recommends installing the update promptly. Loxone has not yet said whether the vulnerability was accessible only on the local network or also over the internet, which Miniserver generations were affected, or whether it was exploited. Starting December 1, Loxone’s remote access service Remote Connect will require at least version 17.2.10.21; users with older software must update to retain remote access.
